[2026-15666: lines 72-341 of 4700, FR page 49230]
    72  SUMMARY: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) is issuing final 
    73  regulations to revise how an employee may appeal a furlough of more 
    74  than 30 days, separation, or demotion by a reduction-in-force (RIF) 
    75  action. OPM will replace the Merit Systems Protection Board (MSPB) as 
    76  the adjudicative agency for such appeals. The rule establishes a 
    77  uniform, record-based OPM appeal process; clarifies the appellant's 
    78  burden; requires production of the complete agency record; preserves 
    79  collateral statutory remedies; and applies prospectively to improve 
    80  timeliness, consistency, and cost-effectiveness while maintaining 
    81  administrative review.
    82  
    83  DATES: Effective September 2, 2026. This final rule applies only to a 
    84  RIF action for which an agency issues the employee a specific RIF 
    85  notice under 5 CFR 351.802 on or after September 2, 2026.
    86  
    87  FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Aaron Gottesman, Senior Advisor to the 
    88  Director, by email at [email protected] or by phone at 
    89  (202) 606-7400.
    90  
    91  SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: OPM is issuing this final rule to modernize 
    92  the administrative process for appeals by employees who are furloughed 
    93  for more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force 
    94  action under 5 CFR part 351. Congress charged OPM with prescribing 
    95  regulations governing the release of competing employees in a RIF, and 
    96  OPM has historically implemented RIF appeal procedures through 
    97  regulation. This final rule revises that regulatory framework by 
    98  replacing the prior MSPB forum for future non-SES RIF appeals with a 
    99  uniform OPM-administered process. The rule does not alter agencies' 
   100  responsibility to determine their workforce needs or whether a RIF is 
   101  necessary. By requiring a complete RIF-specific agency record, 
   102  permitting an appellant reply, authorizing additional information, 
   103  audits, investigations, and hearings when necessary and efficient, and 
   104  preserving collateral statutory remedies, the final rule provides 
   105  meaningful administrative review while reducing delay, fragmentation, 
   106  and unnecessary litigation burden.
   107  
   108  I. Digest of Public Comments and Summary of Changes From the Proposed 
   109  Rule
   110  
   111      In response to the proposed rule, OPM received 1,252 comments 
   112  during the 30-day public comment period from a variety of individuals, 
   113  including current and former civil servants, members of Congress, as 
   114  well as organizations, including local and national unions and Federal 
   115  agencies. Of the 1,252 comments, 1,251 were posted on 
   116  www.regulations.gov, and one was not posted because it contained vulgar 
   117  language unrelated to the rulemaking in question. At the conclusion of 
   118  the public comment period, OPM reviewed and analyzed the comments. In 
   119  general, the comments ranged from ardent support of the proposed 
   120  regulation to categorical rejection of it. Less than 1 percent of the 
   121  overall comments were supportive, neutral, or mixed, and 99 percent 
   122  opposed the proposed regulation.
   123      OPM found many of the comments helpful. OPM has revised the final 
   124  rule to clarify, narrow, or supplement the proposed RIF appeal 
   125  procedures in response to comments, including comments concerning 
   126  burden of proof, access to the agency record, information asymmetry, 
   127  due process, neutrality, hearings, protective orders, collective 
   128  bargaining, and public disclosure. In response to those comments, the 
   129  final rule adds more precise appeal standards, a detailed RIF-specific 
   130  agency-record requirement, disclosure and privilege protections, 
   131  stronger adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards, narrower e-
   132  filing sanctions, more flexible reply rules, and more carefully 
   133  tailored protective order and public posting provisions. The revisions 
   134  are summarized below.
   135      Clarifying appealable actions. The final text clarifies the 
   136  appealable actions set forth in Sec.  351.901(a). The proposal allowed 
   137  an employee ``who has been the subject of a reduction-in-force action'' 
   138  to appeal an action taken under part 351. The final text specifies that 
   139  only an employee furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, or 
   140  demoted by a RIF action taken under part 351 may appeal that action to 
   141  OPM.
   142      Revising the merits standard. The final text replaces the proposed 
   143  ``would not have suffered the same or another RIF action'' standard in 
   144  Sec.  351.901(b) with a more precise two-part merits showing: the 
   145  appellant must prove that the agency failed to comply with an 
   146  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing RIF actions under part 
   147  351, and the failure prejudiced the appellant by causing the appealed 
   148  action or the loss of a materially more favorable outcome. This is 
   149  clearer and better focused on prejudicial RIF-compliance error.
   150      Revising exclusivity language. The final text continues to provide 
   151  that part 351 procedures are the sole and exclusive means of appealing 
   152  a RIF action, and adds that RIFs and matters related to the appeals of 
   153  RIFs cannot be raised in grievance procedures or challenged through 
   154  grievance arbitration, while expressly preserving collateral matters 
   155  within the independent jurisdiction of Equal Employment Opportunity 
   156  Commission (EEOC), Inspectors General, MSPB, Department of Labor 
   157  Veterans' Employment and Training Service (DOL VETS), and the Office of 
   158  Special Counsel (OSC). The final text also retains the no-judicial-
   159  review provision.
   160      Updating filing-system language. The final text replaces the 
   161  proposed placeholder for the electronic filing system with a reference 
   162  to the system identified on OPM's website. It also replaces 
   163  ``statements, evidence, or documents'' with ``pleadings, evidence, or 
   164  documents,'' better aligning the filing provision with adjudicatory 
   165  terminology.
   166      Clarifying filing deadlines. The final text changes the filing 
   167  deadline from 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time to 11:59 p.m. Eastern 
   168  Time, avoiding confusion during daylight saving time. It also 
   169  consolidates the untimely-filing rule in Sec.  351.902(b)(2) and 
   170  provides that good-cause determinations are within OPM's sole and 
   171  exclusive discretion.
   172      Adding a limited tolling rule for collateral matters. The final 
   173  text adds Sec.  351.902(b)(3), which permits an employee who timely 
   174  filed a collateral matter within the independent jurisdiction of an 
   175  entity identified in Sec.  351.901(c) to file a RIF appeal within 30 
   176  calendar days after the final decision on that matter, where that 
   177  decision materially affects the employee's retention standing, order of 
   178  release, assignment rights, or other rights under part 351. The final 
   179  text provides that a decision is final for this purpose when it is no 
   180  longer subject to further administrative review and that OPM 
   181  determines, in its sole and exclusive discretion, whether the decision 
   182  materially affects the employee's rights.
   183      Requiring filing-information detail in the RIF notice. The final 
   184  text amends Sec.  351.802(a)(6) to require the specific RIF notice to 
   185  state, in addition to the employee's right to appeal to OPM, the
   186  
   187  [[Page 49231]]
   188  
   189  time limit for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and the 
   190  electronic filing system through which an appeal must be filed.
   191      Narrowing e-filing enforcement. The final text narrows the proposed 
   192  e-filing enforcement provisions. Rather than authorizing broader orders 
   193  regulating filing methods, sanctions, misuse, or termination of e-filer 
   194  participation, the final text provides that OPM may strike a document 
   195  when an e-filer repeatedly fails to follow filing instructions after a 
   196  show-cause order. The final text also removes the proposed statement 
   197  that withdrawal from e-filing may preclude future re-registration and 
   198  clarifies that withdrawal of e-filing registration is not good cause 
   199  for staying a case.
   200      Simplifying initial-appeal information. The final text simplifies 
   201  the contact-information requirements in Sec.  351.903(a) by replacing 
   202  ``legal name, best address'' with ``name, address.'' The core 
   203  requirement remains unchanged: the appeal must be written, state the 
   204  basis for the appeal, identify the appellant and any representative, 
   205  and include supporting documentation.
   206      Defining the agency record. The final text adds a RIF-specific 
   207  minimum agency-record requirement to Sec.  351.903(b). The proposal 
   208  required the agency response to include the agency record but did not 
   209  define its contents. The final text specifies that the agency record 
   210  includes, at a minimum, the RIF notice and effective-date documents, 
   211  documents supporting the RIF reason, coverage and appointment records, 
   212  competitive-area and competitive-level records, retention-register and 
   213  retention-standing records, order-of-release records, assignment-rights 
   214  records, special RIF-circumstance records, and a certification that the 
   215  complete agency record has been produced.
   216      Distinguishing production to OPM from service on the appellant. The 
   217  final text requires the agency to produce the complete agency record to 
   218  OPM while serving the appellant with the agency record subject to 
   219  legally required limits. The agency may redact or withhold information 
   220  from the appellant's copy only to the extent necessary to comply with 
   221  the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-information or 
   222  national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, or other 
   223  disclosure limits required by law.
   224      Allowing limited new matters in reply. The final text revises Sec.  
   225  351.903(c) to permit an appellant's reply to raise a new allegation of 
   226  error if the basis for that allegation rests on information first 
   227  disclosed in the agency response or if OPM grants leave for good cause.
   228      Adding disclosure limits for inspection and service. The final text 
   229  makes inspection of OPM's appellate record and service of documents 
   230  subject to the Privacy Act, applicable legal privileges, classified-
   231  information or national-security requirements, OPM protective orders, 
   232  and other applicable disclosure limits required by law. The proposal 
   233  allowed inspection and required service but did not include the same 
   234  express disclosure limitations.
   235      Reorganizing representative provisions. The final text reorganizes 
   236  Sec.  351.904 into separate paragraphs addressing designation of a 
   237  representative, Federal employee representatives and restrictions on 
   238  official time and reimbursement, and disallowance of representatives. 
   239  The final text also narrows the grounds for disallowing a 
   240  representative. Because a Federal employee representative may not 
   241  perform representational functions while in a duty status, the final 
   242  text does not adopt the proposed additional grounds for disallowance 
   243  based on the priority needs of the Government or unreasonable costs to 
   244  the Government; OPM or the responsible agency may disallow an 
   245  employee's choice of representative only where the representative is an 
   246  employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the representative's 
   247  activities would cause a conflict of interest or position. The 
   248  remaining changes are primarily organizational and clarifying.
   249      Adding adjudicator-separation and ex parte safeguards. The final 
   250  text adds safeguards in Sec.  351.905(a) requiring OPM adjudicators to 
   251  be insulated from officials who participated personally and 
   252  substantially in the challenged action or provided case-specific 
   253  advice. It also prohibits adjudicators from considering material ex 
   254  parte communications on the merits and requires any such communication 
   255  to be summarized in the record with an opportunity for party response, 
   256  unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
   257      Clarifying OPM employee appeals. The final text clarifies that an 
   258  administrative law judge (ALJ) assigned to adjudicate an OPM employee's 
   259  appeal will issue an initial decision. It also adds material factual 
   260  error affecting the outcome as a ground on which OPM may disturb the 
   261  ALJ's decision and clarifies that assigning an ALJ does not make 5 
   262  U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 applicable unless independently required by law 
   263  or expressly incorporated.
   264      Tightening audits and investigations. The final text narrows the 
   265  standard for OPM audits or investigations. The proposal allowed OPM to 
   266  conduct an audit or investigation when the ``interest of justice'' 
   267  would be served. The final text requires OPM to determine that the 
   268  existing record is insufficient to resolve a material issue within 
   269  OPM's jurisdiction and that the audit or investigation is reasonably 
   270  likely to produce material information. The final text also provides 
   271  that representatives may not participate in an audit or investigation 
   272  unless OPM specifically requests it.
   273      Removing a separate ascertainment sanction. The final text removes 
   274  the proposed separate paragraph authorizing sanctions for failure to 
   275  participate in ascertainment of facts and renumbers the initial-
   276  decision and remedies provisions.
   277      Refining protective-order authority. The final text revises Sec.  
   278  351.906(a). The proposal focused on harassing communications and use of 
   279  appeal information for unrelated purposes. The final text authorizes 
   280  protective orders or cease-and-desist directives to protect the 
   281  integrity of the adjudicatory process and to prevent threats, 
   282  intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness contact, disclosure 
   283  of protected personal information, or misuse of nonpublic information 
   284  obtained through the appeal. It also requires protective orders to be 
   285  no broader than reasonably necessary and not to restrict lawful 
   286  communications protected by law.
   287      Clarifying OPM-initiated reconsideration. The final text clarifies 
   288  in Sec.  351.907(a) that OPM may reopen and reconsider an initial 
   289  decision either upon request of a party or on its own initiative. The 
   290  proposal allowed party-requested reconsideration, while Director sua 
   291  sponte review was addressed separately.
   292      Clarifying Director review. The final text revises Sec.  351.908 to 
   293  preserve the Director's sua sponte authority to reopen and reconsider a 
   294  nonfinal initial decision or reopened and reconsidered decision, while 
   295  identifying nonexclusive considerations that may guide that review. The 
   296  proposal gave the Director broad discretion to reopen and reconsider 
   297  any nonfinal decision. The final text clarifies that the Director may 
   298  consider whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on an 
   299  erroneous material factual finding, involves an issue of exceptional 
   300  importance, affects governmentwide civil service administration, 
   301  conflicts with another OPM decision, or otherwise warrants review. It 
   302  also clarifies that Sec.  351.908 does not create a party right to 
   303  request Director review and that, upon reopening, the Director may take 
   304  any action available under Sec.  351.907(c).
   305  
   306  [[Page 49232]]
   307  
   308      Revising finality of initial decisions. The final text revises 
   309  Sec.  351.909 so that an initial decision becomes final 30 calendar 
   310  days after issuance unless, before that time, a party timely requests 
   311  reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 or the Director 
   312  reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908. A timely request suspends 
   313  finality: if OPM denies or dismisses the request without reopening the 
   314  initial decision, the initial decision becomes final 30 calendar days 
   315  after issuance of the denial or dismissal unless the Director reopens 
   316  it before that time, and if OPM grants the request, the reopened and 
   317  reconsidered decision becomes final 30 calendar days after issuance 
   318  unless the Director reopens that decision before that time. An untimely 
   319  request does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. The final text 
   320  also clarifies that a decision by the Director that disposes of the 
   321  appeal is final and effective upon issuance and that, if the Director 
   322  remands the appeal or directs further proceedings, any resulting 
   323  decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. These changes conform 
   324  finality to the reconsideration and Director-review provisions of the 
   325  final rule.
   326      Adding public-posting disclosure limits. The final text adds 
   327  express legal limits on public posting of final merits decisions, 
   328  including requirements protecting privacy, privileged information, 
   329  protected personnel information, law-enforcement-sensitive information, 
   330  and other information that may not lawfully be disclosed. It also 
   331  clarifies that final merits decisions not publicly posted because of 
   332  such legal limits must be made available upon request to the Federal 
   333  employee or former Federal employee involved in a proceeding under this 
   334  subpart, his or her representative selected pursuant to Sec.  351.904, 
   335  or a representative of the Federal agency or office involved in the 
   336  proceeding who has a need to know.
   337      OPM is finalizing the RIF appeals rule as amended. After 
   338  considering the comments, OPM concludes that the final rule, as 
   339  amended, better balances timely adjudication, governmentwide 
   340  consistency, employee access to meaningful administrative review, and 
   341  agencies' need for finality in workforce restructuring than the current

content.text:
I'm checking the appeal window: the final says 30 calendar days from the effective date, and the separation is Friday, December 18, 2026. Counting from the day after that, December 19 is day 1 and January 17, 2027 is day 30, so I'm checking whether that date falls on a Sunday.

I'm confirming that January 17, 2027 is a Sunday, which pushes the deadline past Martin Luther King Jr. Day on Monday the 18th, so the filing window runs to Tuesday, January 19, 2027 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. I'm also working through which appeal route and notice-date rules apply, since this notice is dated August 31, 2026, before the September 2 effective date of the newer provisions, and I still need to check the RIF appeal specifics. On the burden, I'm noting that the agency must prove the appeal is timely, within jurisdiction, and the procedural noncompliance caused prejudice, by a preponderance of the evidence, and that a hearing isn't automatic.

I'm checking the judicial review point: the regulation text says a party cannot get judicial review of a decision under this subpart, but the preamble discusses judicial review separately, so I want to see whether they differ. I'm also working out the OSC filing deadline, counting 30 calendar days from March 10, 2027, which lands on April 9, 2027.

Now I'm checking the OSC deadline: April 9, 2027 comes out as a Friday, so I'm noting that date at 11:59 p.m. Eastern, but I still need to confirm that OPM decides whether the decision materially affects rights and that the OSC complaint falls under 351.901(c)(3). I'm also checking that the March 10 decision counts as final under the text.

I'm reading through the rest of the appeals text for the RIF provisions, then the preamble sections on judicial review and collective bargaining, so I can compare the final regulation with the proposal. I'll also check correction 17338 and the MSPB appellate jurisdiction update before settling the Q14 comparison.

I'm checking MSPB's own rule text for Q14(iii), and it keys the effective-date cutoff differently in different places: the DATES section looks at when the agency action was taken, the preamble looks at when the RIF notice was issued, and another passage looks at the RIF effective date.

I'm now weighing the case of a RIF with notice on August 31 and an effective date of October 30. Under OPM's notice-based trigger it falls on the cutoff side, but MSPB's DATES language keys on the effective date, which would exclude it, so the two readings conflict.

I'm planning to pull MSPB's lines 100-112 and 176-195 for exact quotes on Q14(iii), plus the 1201.3 amendment text at lines 270-306.

content.text:
I'm checking the MSPB amendment for internal contradictions: instruction 2 removes (a)(3) and (a)(9), yet the preamble refers to amending (a)(6), which is the RIF provision. Instruction 3 then redesignates (a)(4) through (a)(11), moving (a)(6) to (a)(5), and the following step revises that newly redesignated (a)(5).

Now I'm checking whether the preamble's reference to (a)(6) still fits after the redesignation, which it does: the RIF provision moves to (a)(5) and gets revised to cover only furloughs. Then I'm listing the MSPB inconsistencies, starting with the effective-date wording in the DATES section that conflicts with the preamble and section III. Notices issued before September 2 with effective dates on or after that day look like they fall outside both OPM's notice-based rule and MSPB's effective-date criterion.

I'm going through the rest of the MSPB amendment for inconsistencies, including whether its jurisdiction language and the "pending cases" statement still line up with the rest of the rule. Then I plan to check the OPM appeals preamble against its regulatory text, looking at topics like judicial review, grievances, hearings, and filing deadlines.

I'm planning to read the section-by-section discussion of the appeals rule, focusing on the 351.901 and 351.902 parts, and I'll go through roughly that range in the document.

[2026-15666: lines 2279-2608 of 4700, FR page 49247]
  2279  IV. Section-by-Section Analysis
  2280  
  2281      In this section, OPM discusses the regulatory amendments to 5 CFR 
  2282  chapter I, subchapter B, part 351, subpart I, governing appeals of and 
  2283  corrective action with respect to RIFs.
  2284  
  2285  A. Section 351.802--Content of Notice
  2286  
  2287      OPM is revising Sec.  351.802(a)(6), which governs the information 
  2288  an agency must include in a written notice to an employee affected by a 
  2289  reduction in force. Current Sec.  351.802(a)(6) refers to the 
  2290  employee's right to appeal to the Merit Systems Protection Board. 
  2291  Because this final rule transfers adjudication of covered RIF appeals 
  2292  from MSPB to OPM, revised Sec.  351.802(a)(6) replaces the MSPB 
  2293  reference with a reference to OPM.
  2294      The revised provision requires an agency's RIF notice to inform the 
  2295  employee, as applicable, of the employee's right to appeal to OPM. As 
  2296  revised in this final rule, the notice must also state the time limit 
  2297  for filing an appeal under Sec.  351.902(b) and identify the electronic 
  2298  filing system, available on OPM's website, through which an appeal must 
  2299  be filed. This requirement preserves the practical filing information 
  2300  previously conveyed through the cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 of 
  2301  this title and forecloses any contention that a RIF notice failed to 
  2302  apprise an employee of how and when to appeal. The provision is 
  2303  conforming in nature and is intended to ensure that employees receive 
  2304  accurate notice of the administrative appeal forum established by 
  2305  revised subpart I. The revision does not eliminate any independently 
  2306  applicable statutory notice requirement or any separately available 
  2307  remedial process administered by another entity.
  2308      The proposed rule retained legacy language in Sec.  351.802(a)(6) 
  2309  requiring agencies to comply with Sec.  1201.21 of this title, as 
  2310  applicable. OPM is removing that cross-reference in the final rule. 
  2311  Section 1201.21 is an MSPB notice provision that applies when an agency 
  2312  issues a decision notice in a matter appealable to the Board. It 
  2313  requires MSPB-specific information, including notice of the time limits 
  2314  for appealing to the Board, the address of the appropriate Board 
  2315  office, access to the Board's regulations, and access to the MSPB 
  2316  appeal form. Because this final rule replaces MSPB with OPM as the 
  2317  adjudicative forum for RIF appeals under part 351, retaining an 
  2318  unqualified cross-reference to Sec.  1201.21 in the RIF notice 
  2319  provision could create confusion about where an affected employee must 
  2320  file a RIF appeal.
  2321  
  2322  [[Page 49248]]
  2323  
  2324      This deletion is conforming, clarifying, and nonsubstantive. It 
  2325  does not eliminate any appeal right, shorten any filing period, alter 
  2326  the information an agency must provide about the OPM RIF appeal right, 
  2327  or affect any matter that remains independently appealable to MSPB. 
  2328  Rather, it removes an obsolete MSPB-specific notice cross-reference 
  2329  from a provision that now concerns OPM RIF appeals. To the extent an 
  2330  employee has an independent statutory or regulatory right to proceed 
  2331  before MSPB on a collateral matter, that right remains governed by the 
  2332  statutes and regulations applicable to that matter consistent with 
  2333  Sec.  351.901(c).
  2334  
  2335  B. Section 351.807--Certification of Expected Separation
  2336  
  2337      OPM is revising Sec.  351.807(e), which concerns agency 
  2338  determinations of eligibility for certification of expected separation. 
  2339  The prior provision referred to appeal to MSPB. Revised Sec.  
  2340  351.807(e) removes that MSPB reference and states that an agency 
  2341  determination of eligibility for certification may not be appealed.
  2342      This change is also conforming in nature. It aligns Sec.  
  2343  351.807(e) with revised subpart I and clarifies that certification 
  2344  determinations under Sec.  351.807 are not independently appealable 
  2345  under part 351. Employees who are actually furloughed for more than 30 
  2346  days, separated, or demoted by RIF action may pursue any appeal 
  2347  available under revised Sec.  351.901.
  2348  
  2349  C. Subpart I--Appeals
  2350  
  2351      OPM is revising subpart I of part 351 in full. Revised subpart I 
  2352  establishes the procedures governing appeals to OPM by employees who 
  2353  are subject to covered RIF actions. The revised subpart identifies who 
  2354  may appeal, the burden of proof, filing requirements, party 
  2355  submissions, representation rules, adjudication procedures, remedies, 
  2356  sanctions, reconsideration, Director review, and finality.
  2357  1. Section 351.901--Right To Appeal
  2358      Revised Sec.  351.901 establishes the right to appeal a covered 
  2359  reduction-in-force action to OPM, identifies the appellant's burden of 
  2360  proof, and defines the relationship between the OPM RIF appeal process 
  2361  and other remedial forums.
  2362      Paragraph (a) provides that an employee who has been furloughed for 
  2363  more than 30 days, separated, or demoted by a reduction-in-force action 
  2364  taken under part 351 may appeal that action to OPM. This paragraph 
  2365  identifies the covered actions that may be appealed under subpart I and 
  2366  implements the rule's central procedural change: OPM, rather than MSPB, 
  2367  will adjudicate appeals of covered RIF actions, subject to the 
  2368  applicability provision described below.
  2369      Paragraph (b) establishes the employee's burden of proof. The 
  2370  appellant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the 
  2371  written appeal was timely and in the required form; that OPM has 
  2372  jurisdiction over the appeal; that the agency failed to comply with an 
  2373  applicable statute or OPM regulation governing reduction-in-force 
  2374  actions under part 351; and that the failure prejudiced the appellant.
  2375      Paragraph (b)(4) defines the prejudice requirement. The appellant 
  2376  must show that the agency's failure to comply with an applicable RIF 
  2377  statute or OPM regulation caused the appellant to be subjected to the 
  2378  appealed action or to lose a materially more favorable outcome under 
  2379  part 351. This standard is intended to distinguish prejudicial errors 
  2380  from technical or immaterial errors. OPM will not grant relief solely 
  2381  because an agency committed a procedural or technical error if the 
  2382  appellant would have been subject to the same action, or would not have 
  2383  received a materially more favorable outcome, had the agency complied 
  2384  with the applicable requirement. Conversely, prejudice may exist where 
  2385  the violation affected the appellant's retention standing, order of 
  2386  release, assignment rights, notice rights, or other RIF determination 
  2387  in a way that materially affected the outcome of the RIF action as 
  2388  applied to the appellant.
  2389      Paragraph (c)(1) provides that the procedures in part 351 are the 
  2390  sole and exclusive means of appealing a RIF action covered by this 
  2391  subpart. This provision is intended to avoid duplicative or overlapping 
  2392  RIF appeal processes and to channel covered RIF appeals through the OPM 
  2393  procedure established by this final rule. It also promotes consistent 
  2394  application of OPM's governmentwide RIF regulations and avoids parallel 
  2395  adjudication of the same RIF-compliance issues in multiple forums.
  2396      Paragraph (c)(2) provides that a reduction-in-force action taken 
  2397  under part 351, and any matter relating to an appeal of such an action, 
  2398  may not be raised under a negotiated grievance procedure or contested 
  2399  through grievance arbitration. This provision forecloses negotiated 
  2400  grievance procedures and grievance arbitration as alternative forums 
  2401  for direct RIF-compliance challenges, for the reasons discussed in 
  2402  Section III.I of this preamble.
  2403      At the same time, paragraph (c)(3) makes clear that the OPM RIF 
  2404  appeal process does not displace matters within the independent 
  2405  jurisdiction of other entities. Employees may continue to file 
  2406  complaints, appeals, or other matters that fall within the independent 
  2407  jurisdiction of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, an 
  2408  Inspector General, MSPB, the Department of Labor Veterans' Employment 
  2409  and Training Service, or the Office of Special Counsel. Thus, OPM will 
  2410  adjudicate whether the RIF action complied with applicable RIF statutes 
  2411  and OPM regulations, while collateral statutory claims remain available 
  2412  in the forums Congress or applicable law has designated for those 
  2413  claims.
  2414      Paragraph (c)(4) also provides that a party cannot obtain judicial 
  2415  review of a decision under this subpart. OPM addresses comments 
  2416  concerning judicial review and the CSRA remedial scheme in Section 
  2417  III.G.
  2418      Consistent with the DATES section of this preamble, the appeal 
  2419  process established by revised Sec.  351.901 and subpart I is available 
  2420  for a reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued the 
  2421  employee a specific RIF notice under Sec.  351.802 on or after the 
  2422  effective date of the final rule under RIN 3206-AO86. An appeal of a 
  2423  reduction-in-force action for which the agency issued that notice 
  2424  before that date--including an appeal pending before the MSPB--
  2425  continues to be adjudicated by the MSPB under the procedures applicable 
  2426  when the action was taken. This applicability provision is stated in 
  2427  the preamble, and the final regulatory text accordingly does not 
  2428  include a separate applicability note in Sec.  351.901.
  2429  2. Section 351.902--Procedures for Submitting Appeals
  2430      Revised Sec.  351.902 describes the procedures and timeline an 
  2431  employee must adhere to when submitting an appeal.
  2432      Paragraph (a) requires a party, or the party's authorized 
  2433  representative, to file an initial appeal or request for 
  2434  reconsideration through the electronic filing system identified on 
  2435  OPM's website. Unless a party demonstrates good cause and obtains 
  2436  approval from OPM, OPM will not accept pleadings, evidence, or 
  2437  documents submitted by electronic mail or postal mail. This requirement 
  2438  is intended to promote consistent intake, reliable service, accurate 
  2439  case tracking, and efficient adjudication.
  2440      Commenters 0066, 0272, 0296, 0299, 0304, and others, criticized the 
  2441  requirement that employees use e-filing exclusively, absent a showing 
  2442  of good
  2443  
  2444  [[Page 49249]]
  2445  
  2446  cause. OPM disagrees with these criticisms. The good cause requirement 
  2447  permits nonelectronic filing methods for filers with a bona fide need 
  2448  while furthering OPM's legitimate interest in maintaining a streamlined 
  2449  case intake system that minimizes errors and delays. OPM notes that the 
  2450  e-filing requirement for RIF appeals for which this rule provides is 
  2451  consistent with the National Labor Relations Board's policy for 
  2452  requiring parties to e-file documents absent justification to file in 
  2453  paper format.\31\ Other agencies, including the FLRA and OSC, also have 
  2454  adopted restrictions on electronic filing.\32\ OPM acknowledges

  2457  at the time the proposed rule was submitted for public comment. 
  2458  However, OPM is confident that it will have an e-filing system in place 
  2459  by this final rule's effective date.

  2475  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2476  
  2477      Paragraph (b) establishes a 30-calendar-day deadline for filing an 
  2478  appeal. An employee may submit an appeal within 30 calendar days from 
  2479  the effective date of the RIF action. The appeal is timely if 
  2480  electronically filed by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on the 30th calendar 
  2481  day after the effective date of the action.
  2482      Paragraph (b)(1) explains how to compute the filing period. The 
  2483  first day counted is the day after the effective date of the agency 
  2484  action. If the last day for filing falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or 
  2485  Federal holiday, the filing period extends to the first workday after 
  2486  that date.
  2487      Paragraph (b)(2) provides that an untimely appeal will be dismissed 
  2488  unless the employee demonstrates good cause for the untimely filing. 
  2489  OPM will determine good cause in its sole discretion.
  2490      Paragraph (b)(3) adds a limited tolling rule for employees who 
  2491  timely pursue collateral matters. The resolution of a matter within the 
  2492  independent jurisdiction of another entity identified in Sec.  
  2493  351.901(c)--for example, a prohibited-personnel-practice complaint that 
  2494  results in correction of a performance rating--may materially alter an 
  2495  employee's retention standing or other rights under part 351. Paragraph 
  2496  (b)(3) therefore permits an employee who timely filed such a collateral 
  2497  matter to file a RIF appeal within 30 calendar days after the final 
  2498  decision on that matter, where that decision materially affects the 
  2499  employee's retention standing, order of release, assignment rights, or 
  2500  other rights under this part. This provision ensures that an employee 
  2501  is not foreclosed from pursuing a meritorious RIF appeal solely because 
  2502  the predicate for the appeal did not arise until the collateral matter 
  2503  was resolved. For purposes of paragraph (b)(3), a decision on a 
  2504  collateral matter is final when it is no longer subject to further 
  2505  administrative review. OPM will determine, in its sole and exclusive 
  2506  discretion, whether such a decision materially affects the employee's 
  2507  rights under part 351.
  2508      Paragraph (c) establishes e-filing procedures. All parties and 
  2509  representatives must register as instructed by OPM using a unique email 
  2510  address. Registration as an e-filer constitutes consent to electronic 
  2511  service of pleadings, evidence, notices, orders, decisions, and other 
  2512  documents. Parties and representatives may not electronically file 
  2513  documents or access case materials unless registered as e-filers.
  2514      The e-filing system will make OPM-issued documents and party-filed 
  2515  documents available for viewing and downloading, with access limited to 
  2516  the parties and their representatives in the relevant case. Parties and 
  2517  representatives must follow OPM's filing instructions. OPM may strike a 
  2518  document if an e-filer repeatedly fails to follow those instructions 
  2519  after issuance of a show-cause order.
  2520      Paragraph (c) also requires e-filers to keep their contact 
  2521  information current, notify OPM and other parties of changes in 
  2522  address, telephone number, or email address by filing a pleading in 
  2523  each pending case, and regularly monitor case activity in the e-filing 
  2524  system. A party or representative may withdraw e-filing registration in 
  2525  accordance with OPM's posted requirements. After OPM processes a proper 
  2526  withdrawal, the person will no longer receive electronic service or 
  2527  have electronic access to case records through the e-filing system. OPM 
  2528  may continue processing the appeal or reconsideration request after 
  2529  withdrawal, and withdrawal will not be considered good cause for 
  2530  staying a case.
  2531      OPM may, in its sole and exclusive discretion, exempt a party or 
  2532  representative from registering as an e-filer for good cause. A party 
  2533  or representative seeking an exemption must promptly contact OPM as 
  2534  instructed on OPM's website. OPM will not find good cause for failing 
  2535  to timely file an appeal or seek reconsideration if the party or 
  2536  representative failed to contact OPM to request an exemption before the 
  2537  applicable deadline. Documents filed through OPM's e-filing system are 
  2538  deemed received on the date of electronic submission.
  2539  3. Section 351.903--Form and Content of RIF Appeal and Agency Response
  2540      Revised Sec.  351.903 identifies the required contents of the 
  2541  employee's appeal, the agency's response, the agency record, any 
  2542  employee reply, inspection of OPM's appellate record, service 
  2543  requirements, and treatment of untimely filings.
  2544      Paragraph (a) requires the employee's appeal to be in writing and 
  2545  to state the basis for the appeal. The appeal must include the name, 
  2546  address, and email address or telephone number of the appellant and, if 
  2547  applicable, the appellant's representative. The employee must also 
  2548  include any documentation supporting the appeal.
  2549      Paragraph (b) requires the agency to file its response within 30 
  2550  calendar days after service of the initial appeal. The agency response 
  2551  must identify the appellant and the agency whose action is being 
  2552  appealed; identify the reduction-in-force action taken against the 
  2553  appellant and state the reasons for the action; include all documents 
  2554  contained in the agency record of the action; designate and be signed 
  2555  by the authorized agency representative; and include any other 
  2556  documents or responses requested by OPM.
  2557      Paragraph (b) also identifies the minimum contents of the agency 
  2558  record for a RIF appeal. The agency record must include, at a minimum

  2560  amended notice, proof of service or receipt, and documents showing the 
  2561  effective date of the action. The record must also include documents

I'm comparing the preamble's description of paragraph (b) with the published text. The preamble says the appellant must show the written appeal was timely and in the required form, but the text of (b)(1) only mentions timeliness, so "in the required form" is an addition the text doesn't have. I'm also checking (c)(1), where the preamble refers to part 351 procedures but the published text says "this part," and the correction I'm making points to "this sub..."

I'm checking the remaining preamble points against the published text: the applicability date matches, the "good cause" discretion wording differs only trivially, and the 351.802 and 351.807 references look consistent. Next I still need to compare the preamble sections covering 351.904 through 351.909, plus the judicial review and collective bargaining parts.

I'm working through the remaining appeals preamble now, with a rough budget in mind: the appeals proposal text, the main proposed rule text, the final rule's Q13 material, and the CBA preamble, then the answer itself. Next I'll read the appeals preamble from line 2609 to 2900.

  2652  appeals under this subpart.
  2653      Paragraph (c) authorizes OPM or the responsible agency to disallow 
  2654  a representative in specified circumstances. OPM or the agency may 
  2655  disallow the employee's choice of representative when the 
  2656  representative is an employee of the responsible agency or OPM and the 
  2657  representative's activities would cause a conflict of interest or 
  2658  position. Because paragraph (b) prohibits a Federal employee 
  2659  representative from performing representational functions while in a 
  2660  duty status, the final rule does not adopt the proposed additional 
  2661  grounds for disallowance based on the priority needs of the Government 
  2662  or unreasonable costs to the Government.
  2663  5. Section 351.905--Adjudication of Appeals
  2664      Revised Sec.  351.905 establishes the procedures for adjudicating 
  2665  RIF appeals.
  2666      Paragraph (a) governs appeals by employees of agencies other than 
  2667  OPM. OPM will assign personnel to adjudicate those appeals. Assigned 
  2668  OPM personnel must be insulated from officials who participated 
  2669  personally and substantially in the challenged personnel action or 
  2670  provided case-specific advice concerning that action. OPM adjudicators 
  2671  may not consider material ex parte communications concerning the merits 
  2672  of an appeal. If such a communication occurs, OPM will place a summary 
  2673  of the communication in the record and provide the parties a reasonable 
  2674  opportunity to respond, unless disclosure is prohibited by law.
  2675      Paragraph (a) also establishes assignment restrictions. No OPM 
  2676  employee may be assigned to adjudicate an appeal if the employee has a 
  2677  relationship with the appellant or, during the preceding two years, was 
  2678  an employee of the agency that is a party to the appeal or was subject 
  2679  to an action covered under part 351. When necessary, OPM may assign an 
  2680  administrative law judge to preside over the adjudication of an appeal 
  2681  by a non-OPM employee.
  2682      Paragraph (b) establishes a separate procedure for appeals by OPM 
  2683  employees. OPM will assign an administrative law judge to adjudicate
  2684  
  2685  [[Page 49251]]
  2686  
  2687  an appeal by an OPM employee. The administrative law judge will issue 
  2688  an initial decision. To insulate adjudication of OPM employees' appeals 
  2689  from agency involvement, OPM will not disturb the initial decision in 
  2690  those cases unless a party shows a harmful procedural irregularity 
  2691  before the administrative law judge, a clear error of law, or a 
  2692  material factual error that affected the outcome of the appeal.
  2693      Under this construction, the OPM Director would be proactively 
  2694  exercising restraint in permitting decisions pertaining to OPM 
  2695  employees to lie undisturbed, not delegating his authority to the ALJ. 
  2696  In essence, the OPM Director is regulatorily tying his own hands but 
  2697  can nevertheless choose to regulatorily untie them. This leaves the ALJ 
  2698  as a properly supervised inferior officer, not a principal officer. See 
  2699  United States v. Arthrex, Inc., 594 U.S. 1, 6 (2021) (holding that the 
  2700  Appointments Clause provides that inferior officers may exercise 
  2701  executive power provided they are directed and supervised by a 
  2702  principal officer.).
  2703      Paragraph (b) defines ``harmful procedural irregularity'' as an 
  2704  irregularity in the application of procedures likely to have caused the 
  2705  administrative law judge to reach a conclusion different from the one 
  2706  the judge would have reached in the absence or cure of the 
  2707  irregularity. The assignment of an administrative law judge under 
  2708  paragraphs (a) or (b) does not make 5 U.S.C. 554, 556, or 557 
  2709  applicable to an appeal under part 351, except to the extent those 
  2710  provisions are independently required by law or expressly incorporated 
  2711  in the rule.
  2712      Paragraph (c) addresses ascertainment of facts. OPM may require 
  2713  either party to provide additional information. OPM may also audit or 
  2714  investigate an agency's action if OPM determines, in its sole 
  2715  discretion, that the existing record is insufficient to resolve a 
  2716  material issue within OPM's jurisdiction and that an audit or 
  2717  investigation is reasonably likely to produce information material to 
  2718  resolving that issue. A representative of either party may not 
  2719  participate in an audit or investigation unless OPM specifically 
  2720  requests that participation.
  2721      The review of an agency action will be based on the developed 
  2722  written record unless OPM determines that a hearing is necessary and 
  2723  efficient. Paragraph (c) defines ``necessary and efficient'' to mean 
  2724  circumstances in which the written record is insufficiently developed 
  2725  to determine one or more facts material to the outcome of the appeal, 
  2726  or where there is a disputed issue of witness credibility that is 
  2727  material to the outcome. If OPM conducts an investigation or audit, OPM 
  2728  will inform the employee, the employee's representative, and the 
  2729  agency, provide them the results, and give them a reasonable 
  2730  opportunity to submit arguments or additional information supporting 
  2731  their positions.
  2732      Paragraph (d) requires OPM to notify the employee, the employee's 
  2733  representative, and the agency in writing of its decision.
  2734      Paragraph (e) addresses remedies. If the employee is the prevailing 
  2735  party, OPM will order relief, including correction of the personnel 
  2736  action and any back pay, interest, and reasonable attorney fees 
  2737  consistent with subpart H of part 550 of this chapter. The employee is 
  2738  not entitled to compensatory damages or other relief not authorized 
  2739  under 5 U.S.C. 5596(b).
  2740      Paragraph (e) also provides that if the agency timely requests 
  2741  reconsideration of an initial decision or OPM reopens and reconsiders 
  2742  an initial decision, the agency must continue to provide the relief 
  2743  ordered unless OPM issues an order staying that relief. OPM may not 
  2744  order a stay that would deprive the employee of pay and benefits while 
  2745  the initial decision is pending reconsideration.
  2746  6. Section 351.906--Sanctions and Protective Orders
  2747      Revised Sec.  351.906 authorizes OPM to issue protective orders and 
  2748  cease-and-desist directives, and identifies available consequences for 
  2749  noncompliance. OPM stated in the proposed rule that it believes that 
  2750  MSPB procedures, while providing for protective orders, are inadequate 
  2751  to protect Federal employees from threats and harassment.
  2752      Paragraph (a) permits OPM to issue a protective order or cease-and-
  2753  desist directive to protect the integrity of the adjudicatory process, 
  2754  prevent threats, intimidation, targeted harassment, improper witness 
  2755  contact, disclosure of protected personal information, or misuse of 
  2756  nonpublic information obtained through the appeal. OPM may act sua 
  2757  sponte or at the request of a party, either preemptively or at any 
  2758  point in the appeal process.
  2759      A party requesting a protective order or cease-and-desist directive 
  2760  must file the request through the prescribed e-filing procedures and 
  2761  include a statement of reasons supporting the request, along with 
  2762  relevant documentary evidence. Any protective order issued by OPM must 
  2763  be no broader than reasonably necessary and must not restrict lawful 
  2764  communications protected by law.
  2765      Commenters 0442, 0443, 0513, and 1119 objected to section 
  2766  351.906(a) of the proposed rule, asserting the standards under which it 
  2767  permitted OPM to issue cease-and-desist directives were overly broad 
  2768  and vague such that it would chill employees from exercising their 
  2769  First Amendment right to speak publicly about RIF adjudications.
  2770      OPM has considered these comments and is narrowing Sec.  351.906 in 
  2771  the final rule. The final rule does not adopt the broad ``reasonably be 
  2772  foreseen to lead to harassment'' formulation and does not authorize OPM 
  2773  to bar use of any information related to an appeal for any purpose 
  2774  whatsoever. Instead, OPM may issue a protective order or cease-and-
  2775  desist directive only to protect the integrity of the adjudicatory 
  2776  process; prevent threats, intimidation, targeted harassment, improper 
  2777  witness contact, disclosure of protected personal information; or 
  2778  prevent misuse of nonpublic information obtained through the appeal. 
  2779  The final rule also adds two limiting principles. Any protective order 
  2780  must be no broader than reasonably necessary, and any such order must 
  2781  not restrict lawful communications protected by law.
  2782      OPM declines to remove protective-order authority entirely. Because 
  2783  OPM will adjudicate appeals under subpart I of part 351, it must have 
  2784  reasonable procedural tools to protect witnesses, parties, protected 
  2785  personal information, nonpublic appeal materials, and the integrity of 
  2786  the adjudicatory record. OPM also retains authority to act sua sponte 
  2787  or preemptively where necessary, because threats to the process, 
  2788  improper witness contact, or disclosure of protected information may 
  2789  arise before a party files a motion or before harm has fully occurred. 
  2790  That authority is limited to matters connected to an appeal under 
  2791  subpart I of part 351 and to the specific purposes identified in Sec.  
  2792  351.906(a).
  2793      Paragraph (b) identifies consequences for failure to comply with an 
  2794  OPM directive issued under paragraph (a). Except where prohibited by 
  2795  law, OPM may draw inferences against the noncompliant party, prohibit 
  2796  the noncompliant party from introducing evidence or additional evidence 
  2797  or otherwise relying on the record, or eliminate from consideration an 
  2798  appropriate part of the noncompliant party's filings or submissions.
  2799      OPM is additionally specifying in paragraph (c) that any sanction 
  2800  issued under paragraph (b) must be proportionate, causally related to 
  2801  the violation, and no broader than necessary to protect the 
  2802  adjudicatory process.
  2803  
  2804  [[Page 49252]]
  2805  
  2806  7. Section 351.907--Reconsideration of an Initial Decision
  2807      Revised Sec.  351.907 establishes the process for reconsideration 
  2808  of an initial decision.
  2809      Paragraph (a) authorizes OPM, in its sole discretion, to reopen and 
  2810  reconsider an initial decision upon request of either party or on OPM's 
  2811  own initiative. An employee, the employee's representative, or the 
  2812  agency may request reconsideration within 30 calendar days from 
  2813  issuance of the initial decision. The request must be filed in the same 
  2814  manner as an initial appeal.
  2815      Paragraph (b) identifies the grounds on which OPM may grant 
  2816  reconsideration. OPM may grant reconsideration if the initial decision 
  2817  contains erroneous findings of material fact sufficient to warrant a 
  2818  different outcome; if the initial decision is based on an erroneous 
  2819  interpretation of statute or regulation or an erroneous application of 
  2820  law to the facts; if new and material evidence or legal argument is 
  2821  available that, despite the party's due diligence, was not available 
  2822  when the record closed; or if OPM finds good cause to reconsider the 
  2823  appeal.
  2824      When a party alleges legal error, the party must explain how the 
  2825  error affected the outcome of the case. For new evidence, the relevant 
  2826  question is whether the information contained in the documents, not 
  2827  merely the documents themselves, was unavailable despite due diligence 
  2828  when the record closed.
  2829      Paragraph (c) describes OPM's authority in a reopened or reviewed 
  2830  case. OPM may issue a reopened and reconsidered decision that affirms, 
  2831  reverses, modifies, vacates, or otherwise decides the case in whole or 
  2832  in part. OPM may require the parties to submit argument and evidence, 
  2833  take any other action necessary for final disposition of the case, and 
  2834  issue an order with a date for compliance.
  2835      Paragraph (d) provides that there is no further right of 
  2836  administrative appeal from the reopened and reconsidered decision.
  2837  8. Section 351.908--Review by the OPM Director
  2838      Section 351.908 reserves to the OPM Director the authority, in the 
  2839  Director's discretion and sua sponte, to reopen and reconsider any 
  2840  appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not yet become 
  2841  final. Once a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909, Sec.  351.908 
  2842  does not provide a separate mechanism for reopening that decision.
  2843      Many commenters (including 0177, 0395, 0411, 0555, 1020, and 
  2844  others) objected to providing the OPM Director with the authority to 
  2845  reopen and reconsider decisions at his or her direction, sua sponte, 
  2846  contending that it violated due process.
  2847      In response to comments expressing concern that Director review 
  2848  could be too open-ended or could undermine the perceived neutrality of 
  2849  OPM adjudication, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify 
  2850  nonexclusive considerations that may inform the Director's decision to 
  2851  reopen and reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision. Under the final 
  2852  rule, the Director may act on the Director's own initiative and only 
  2853  before a decision becomes final under Sec.  351.909. In determining 
  2854  whether to exercise that authority, the Director may consider, among 
  2855  other things, whether the decision contains clear legal error, rests on 
  2856  an erroneous finding of material fact, involves an issue of exceptional 
  2857  importance, affects the governmentwide administration of civil service 
  2858  laws, rules, regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM 
  2859  decision, or otherwise warrants Director review.
  2860      This revision responds to commenters who objected to Director 
  2861  review as insufficiently cabined, while preserving final agency 
  2862  supervision over important legal, factual, policy, consistency, and 
  2863  governmentwide civil service issues. OPM has retained sua sponte 
  2864  Director review because final agency oversight promotes decisional 
  2865  consistency and accountability within OPM's adjudicatory process. The 
  2866  revision does not create a separate right for parties to request 
  2867  Director review; parties may seek reconsideration under Sec.  351.907. 
  2868  If the Director reopens and reconsiders a decision under Sec.  351.908, 
  2869  the Director may take any action available under Sec.  351.907(c). This 
  2870  structure preserves meaningful principal-officer oversight while 
  2871  clarifying that Director review will occur within the rule's record-
  2872  based adjudicatory framework, including the final rule's agency-record, 
  2873  separation-of-functions, ex parte, reconsideration, and finality 
  2874  provisions.
  2875      OPM declines to eliminate Director review entirely. Director review 
  2876  serves both administrative and constitutional functions. As an 
  2877  administrative matter, it ensures that OPM can correct material legal, 
  2878  factual, or procedural errors before a decision becomes final; resolve 
  2879  recurring or important questions of interpretation; and promote uniform 
  2880  application of part 351 across agencies. That review function is 
  2881  especially important in a governmentwide personnel system, where 
  2882  inconsistent interpretations by subordinate adjudicators could produce 
  2883  uneven appeal rights for similarly situated employees in different 
  2884  agencies. Cf. 5 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1), (3), (5) (vesting the OPM Director 
  2885  with responsibility for securing ``accuracy, uniformity, and justice'' 
  2886  in OPM's functions, directing and supervising OPM employees, and 
  2887  executing, administering, and enforcing civil-service laws and 
  2888  regulations).
  2889      Director review also reinforces the rule's consistency with the 
  2890  Appointments Clause. The Constitution requires principal officers to be 
  2891  appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, 
  2892  while Congress may vest appointment of inferior officers in the 
  2893  President alone, courts of law, or heads of departments. U.S. Const. 
  2894  art. II, Sec.  2, cl. 2. The OPM Director is a presidentially 
  2895  appointed, Senate-confirmed officer. 5 U.S.C. 1102(a). Under the 
  2896  Supreme Court's Appointments Clause precedents, inferior officers must 
  2897  remain subject to direction and supervision by a properly appointed 
  2898  superior officer. Edmond v. United States, 520 U.S. 651, 663-65 (1997). 
  2899  In the adjudicatory context, the Court has treated the availability of 
  2900  review by a superior executive officer as a significant feature 
  2901  distinguishing inferior officers from principal officers. Id. at 665.
  2902      That principle is particularly relevant where subordinate 
  2903  adjudicators exercise significant authority under Federal law. The 
  2904  Supreme Court has held that officials who occupy continuing offices and 
  2905  exercise significant discretion in conducting adjudications may be 
  2906  ``Officers of the United States'' rather than mere employees. See 
  2907  Freytag v. Comm'r, 501 U.S. 868, 881-82 (1991); Lucia v. SEC, 585 U.S. 
  2908  237, 245-51 (2018). The rule preserves supervision by the Director, a 
  2909  principal officer, before OPM's decision becomes final. Consistent with 
  2910  Freytag, Lucia, and related precedents, the Director will appoint, or 
  2911  ratify the appointments of, the OPM personnel assigned to adjudicate 
  2912  appeals under this subpart, ensuring that any adjudicator who exercises 
  2913  significant authority as an inferior officer has been properly 
  2914  appointed.
  2915      The Supreme Court's decision in United States v. Arthrex, 594 U.S. 
  2916  1, 22-23 (2021), confirms the importance of that structure. There, the 
  2917  Court held that administrative patent judges could not constitutionally 
  2918  issue unreviewable final decisions on behalf of the Executive Branch 
  2919  while being appointed only as inferior officers. The constitutional 
  2920  problem was not that subordinate adjudicators participated in deciding 
  2921  cases; it was that their decisions were insulated from review by
  2922  
  2923  [[Page 49253]]
  2924  
  2925  a principal officer. Id. at 25-26. The Court's remedy was to permit 
  2926  discretionary review by the Director of the Patent and Trademark 
  2927  Office, explaining that the Director need not review every decision, 
  2928  but must have authority to review decisions if he chooses. Id. at 27-
  2929  28.
  2930      The appeals process established in this rule follows that model. 
  2931  OPM adjudicators may issue initial decisions, and OPM may reopen and 
  2932  reconsider those decisions on party request or on its own initiative. 
  2933  In addition, the Director may, in his or her discretion, reopen and 
  2934  reconsider any appeal in which OPM has issued a decision that has not 
  2935  yet become final, and a decision issued by the Director is the final 
  2936  decision of OPM. This structure ensures that no subordinate adjudicator 
  2937  has unreviewable authority to bind OPM or the Executive Branch in an 
  2938  appeal under subpart I of part 351.
  2939      OPM does not agree that the possibility of Director review 
  2940  establishes bias or a due-process violation. Agency heads commonly 
  2941  retain final decisional authority within administrative adjudication 
  2942  systems, and the mere availability of final agency review does not show 
  2943  prejudgment, bad faith, or inability to decide a matter fairly.\33\ The 
  2944  Director's review authority applies only before a decision becomes 
  2945  final. It does not permit adjudication outside the regulatory 
  2946  framework, and it does not eliminate the requirement that decisions be 
  2947  based on the record and the governing standards in part 351. In 
  2948  addition, OPM has revised Sec.  351.908 to identify nonexclusive 
  2949  considerations that may inform the Director's decision to reopen and 
  2950  reconsider a nonfinal RIF appeal decision, including whether the 
  2951  decision contains clear legal error, rests on an erroneous finding of 
  2952  material fact, involves an issue of exceptional importance, affects the 
  2953  governmentwide administration of civil service laws, rules, 
  2954  regulations, or OPM policy, conflicts with another OPM decision, or 
  2955  otherwise warrants Director review.
  2956  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2957  
  2958      \33\ See Fogo de Chao (Holdings) Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Homeland 
  2959  Sec., 769 F.3d 1127, 1148-49 (D.C. Cir. 2014) (declining to find a 
  2960  due process violation where plaintiff did not establish that the 
  2961  individual agency decisionmaker ``ha[d] a closed mind'' and was 
  2962  ``impervious to evidence or argument''); Riggins v. Goodman, 572 
  2963  F.3d 1101, 1115 (10th Cir. 2009) (denying claim of due process 
  2964  violation absent evidence that administrative adjudicators had a 
  2965  pecuniary interest in the case or personal animosity against a 
  2966  party).
  2967  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  2968  
  2969      The final rule thus ensures that Director review occurs within a 
  2970  structured adjudicatory process that includes record-based decision-
  2971  making, separation-of-functions protections, ex parte safeguards, 
  2972  reconsideration, and public availability of final merits decisions. 
  2973  Commenters did not identify specific evidence that the OPM Director 
  2974  would prejudge individual RIF appeals or direct outcomes contrary to 
  2975  the record. OPM therefore declines to eliminate Director review.
  2976  9. Section 351.909--Final Decision
  2977      Revised Sec.  351.909 explains when decisions issued under subpart 
  2978  I become final and the effect of finality.
  2979      Paragraph (a) provides that an initial decision becomes OPM's final 
  2980  decision 30 calendar days after issuance unless, before that time, a 
  2981  party timely requests reopening and reconsideration under Sec.  351.907 
  2982  or the Director reopens the decision under Sec.  351.908.
  2983      Paragraph (b) provides that a timely request for reconsideration 
  2984  under Sec.  351.907 suspends finality. If OPM denies or dismisses the 
  2985  request without reopening the initial decision, the initial decision 
  2986  becomes OPM's final decision 30 calendar days after issuance of the 
  2987  denial or dismissal, unless the Director reopens the initial decision 
  2988  under Sec.  351.908 before that time. If OPM grants the request, the 
  2989  reopened and reconsidered decision becomes OPM's final decision 30 
  2990  calendar days after issuance unless the Director reopens that decision 
  2991  under Sec.  351.908 before that time.
  2992      Paragraph (c) provides that an untimely request under Sec.  351.907 
  2993  does not suspend or otherwise affect finality. If OPM accepts and 
  2994  grants an untimely request for good cause, any resulting reopened and 
  2995  reconsidered decision becomes final as provided in paragraph (b).
  2996      Paragraph d) provides that a decision by the Director under Sec.  
  2997  351.908 that disposes of the appeal is OPM's final decision and is 
  2998  effective upon issuance. If the Director remands the appeal or directs 
  2999  further proceedings, any resulting decision becomes final under Sec.  
  3000  351.909.
  3001      Paragraph (e) states that there is no further right of appeal of a 
  3002  final decision of OPM. This provision works together with Sec.  
  3003  351.901(c), which establishes the OPM process as the sole and exclusive 
  3004  means of appealing covered RIF actions under part 351 and provides that 
  3005  a party cannot obtain judicial review of a decision under this subpart.
  3006      As stated above, OPM is limiting judicial review of decisions 
  3007  issued under this subpart to adhere to the CSRA's specific and well-
  3008  defined statutory scheme for judicial review and prevent unnecessarily

content.text:
I'm comparing the Q14(i) preamble against the corrected text. The preamble's 351.904(c) says "OPM or the responsible agency may disallow," while the corrected text says "agency whose action is under appeal," which is a minor terminology difference I might mention with low confidence. I'm also starting to look at the 351.905(b) preamble language about OPM not disturbing the initial decision unless there is harmful procedural irregularity.

I'm checking the remaining Federal Register preamble points against the corrected text, looking at the 351.905 and 351.908 language, which seems to match, and the 351.907(a) 30-day reconsideration window. I'm also comparing 351.901(c)(1) and 351.901(b), where the preamble refers to "part 351" and a "required form" that the text wording doesn't carry over.

I'm going through the rest of the preamble-to-text checks for Q14(i): the 351.902(b) filing deadline and electronic-filing cutoff, the 351.903(a) contact information, and the summary points on tolling and exclusivity, which all look consistent with the corrected text.

I'm checking the remaining preamble points against the corrected text: the 351.901(b) filing deadline and electronic-filing cutoff, the 351.902(b)(3) 30-day window, and the 351.903(a) contact details all line up. I'm also noting that the preamble says the rule applies only to RIF notices issued on or after the effective date, with pending MSPB appeals staying there. One thing I'm unsure about is the "non-SES" wording in the introduction, since the corrected 351.901(a) text doesn't seem to exclude SES employees.

I'm still checking the preamble against the text: the Foreign Service jurisdiction point means MSPB keeps its role there, which the abstract's wording doesn't capture. Next I need to look at the preamble sections on collective bargaining agreements and judicial review.

I'm comparing the preamble's statement that the rule won't retroactively invalidate existing CBAs, and that it limits agencies' duty only once agreements are renegotiated, against section 351.901(c)(2), which bars raising these matters under a negotiated grievance procedure and applies to RIF notices issued on or after September 2 regardless of renegotiation. These seem to point in different directions, so I'm checking whether that is a real preamble-versus-text mismatch.

I'm going to skip the exact decision statement at lines 1845-1870, since I already have the key conflict. Next I'll search the preamble for judicial review language such as "APA", "5 U.S.C. 704", or "judicial review", to see whether it says anything about review under the APA.

I'm checking the text of 351.901(c)(4) and 351.909(e), which bar judicial review of decisions under this subpart. The preamble says the rule doesn't withdraw review Congress provided, which conflicts with that text, so I'm flagging it. On the text, the answer to (e) is no, though the preamble's "eliminates" language is disputed, and collateral claims in other forums stay open. Next I'm turning to the proposed appeals rule 2026-02576 text for Q14(ii).

I'm going to locate the regulatory text of the proposed rule, searching for the Part 351 sections, and read from the start of Part 351 using a small table-of-contents lookup.

content.text:
I'm checking the proposed-to-final changes that the summary left out. The proposed 351.901(c) said the procedures "shall supersede" agency policies and collective bargaining appeal procedures, and the final rule dropped "supersede" for a grievance prohibition, which arguably still amounts to acknowledged exclusivity. The final also removed the Federal Labor Relations Authority from the entities listed in (c)(3).

I'm comparing the proposed and final texts for changes the summary doesn't mention. The FLRA was dropped from the list of entities in (c)(3), and the summary doesn't say so. I also see that "hearing or any other appropriate action" was cut from 351.905(c), that OPM gained power to require additional information, and that the audit standard went from "sole and exclusive discretion" to "sole discretion."

I'm checking the rest of the proposed-to-final comparison: the mandatory "OPM shall" in 351.906(b) became "OPM may," and a proportionality limit on sanctions appears in (c) that the summary doesn't mention. I'm also noting that the authority citation picked up new statutory references, which the correction document may explain.

I'm now checking the proposed-to-final changes on the e-filing exemption: the final rule's (c)(2) adds an exemption under (c)(7) for good cause, which the summary doesn't mention. I'm also noting that the 30-day response period in 351.903(b)(1) shifted from running from the initial appeal to running from service of it, another change the summary leaves out.

I'm going through the rest of the proposed-to-final comparison: the 351.904 reorganization and narrowed disallowance, the insulation and ex parte language in 351.905(a), and the "material factual error" addition in 351.905(b) all look acknowledged, as do the 351.908 and 351.802(a)(6) changes. I'm also checking the 351.903(c) reply limit on new allegations of error, which the summary does cover.

I'm checking whether the final rule's good-cause exemption for e-filing, and the shift in the 30-day response trigger, are things the summary leaves out. I'm also checking whether the new good-cause acceptance for untimely requests in 351.909(c) is covered, since the summary only mentions that an untimely request doesn't affect finality.

I'm now comparing the preamble's statements about the rule against the regulatory text. The preamble says the procedures are the exclusive means, but the text, as corrected, refers to "this subpart" rather than "this part." I'm also checking the preamble's claim that existing collective bargaining agreements aren't retroactively invalidated and that the limit applies only on renegotiation, against what the text actually says in 351.901(c)(2).

I'm checking the preamble's statements against the regulatory text, and the next item is the 351.904(c) wording, where the preamble names OPM or the responsible agency but the corrected text names only the agency whose action is under appeal. I'm also noting that the preamble's account of 351.908 on reopening and reconsidering appeals continues past where the thinking stops.

I'm now checking the preamble's claims against the text: the judicial review language, where the preamble says Congress's review is preserved but (c)(4) bars it, and a point about the applicability section that cuts off before it finishes.

I'm checking the applicability dates against the preamble: the rule covers RIF notices issued on or after September 2, 2026, which matches the effective date in Section IV. Next I'm comparing the Board's own rule against OPM's, since OPM keys coverage to the notice date while the Board's DATES language is framed around when agency actions were taken.

I'm now checking the MSPB rule's description of OPM's rule, which says it removes MSPB appeal rights, and the claim that the appeal right is kept in redesignated paragraph (a)(5), and both look consistent. I'm also noting that the MSPB summary describes the Foreign Service jurisdiction point correctly against OPM's 351.901. Then I'm checking the 1201.3(a)(6) amendment against the instruction, which seems to remove only (a)(3) and (a)(9).

Now I'm comparing the proposed rule's regulatory text against the final version, so I'll look at the proposed part 351 provisions next.

I'm moving on to the proposed Part 351 regulatory text, setting aside the other parts of the rule, and looking for where those provisions start.

content.text:
I'm comparing the proposed rule against the final version, starting with the authority citations: the final one adds 2301 and 38 U.S.C. 4331 to the list. Next is the wording in 351.202(c)(3), where the proposed text has a stray "such" that the final version drops. I'm also starting to look at the heading of 351.202(d) on excluded employees.

Next I'm checking the exclusion categories in 351.202(d): the heading and intro change, and the trial-period and appointment conditions in (d)(1) and (d)(2) lose their date language or narrow their scope. The (d)(3) catch-all is also much narrower in the final version.

Next I'm going through the rest of the diff, section 351.203: the furlough definition drops the "dependent entirely on congressional action" clause, the probationary and military spouse references get corrected back to "of this chapter," and the rating-of-record wording and the 430.208 cross-reference change. I'm also noting the new "restoration protected employee" definition and starting on 351.204's added language about regulations being administered consistent with merit system principles.

I'm now going through the remaining sections of the regulation diff: the wording of 351.302(d) on adverse action procedures changes from a reference to part 752 to a broader list that includes procedures required by law or regulation, and I'm noting the smaller wording changes in (g). Then I'm checking 351.402, where the final version adds a new paragraph (c) on OPM approval of competitive area changes within 90 days.

I'm checking the Section 351.502 changes next: the trigger moves from when the agency issues the RIF notice to when the employee receives it, and the reference to subparts C and D of part 316 is narrowed to subpart D.

tools.name: fr_search

query.description: Full-text search terms; "" for none. Supports quoted phrases, e.g. "\"extension of stay\" F-1".

tools.name: fr_doc
tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty
